'''''Ficus pumila''''', commonly known as the '''creeping fig''' or '''climbing fig''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Moraceae|mulberry family]], native to [[East Asia]] (southern China, southern Japan,southern Korea, Vietnam)<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=233500650 Flora of China, ''Ficus pumila'' Linnaeus, 1753.  <big>薜荔</big> bi li ]</ref> and [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in parts of the southeastern and south-central United States.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=233500650 Flora of North America, ''Ficus pumila'' Linnaeus, 1753. Climbing fig ]</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Ficus%20pumila.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref> It is also found in cultivation as a [[houseplant]]. The Latin [[specific epithet]] ''pumila'' means "dwarf",<ref>{{cite book |language=fr |last=Gaffiot |first=Félix |date=1934 |title=Dictionnaire illustré Latin-Français |place=Paris |publisher=Librairie Hachette |page=1278 |url=http://www.lexilogos.com/latin/gaffiot.php?q=pumilus |access-date=23 October 2016}}</ref> and refers to the very small leaves of the plant.

==Description==
''Ficus pumila'' is a woody [[evergreen]] [[liana]], growing to {{convert|2.5|-|12|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall.<ref>[https://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/2029/#b Ficus Species, Climbing Fig, Creeping Ficus, Creeping Fig] by Dave's Garden</ref> The juvenile foliage is much smaller and thinner than mature leaves produced as the plant ages. The leaves are oval, cordate, asymmetrical, with opposite veins. It is creeping or can behave like a [[liana]] and also climb trees, rocks, etc. up to 4 m in height or more. The [[aerial root]]s secrete a translucent [[latex]] that hardens on drying, allowing the stems to adhere to their support.{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}}

It is pollinated by the fig wasp ''[[Wiebesia pumilae]]'' (syn. ''Blastophaga pumilae''), and is fed upon by [[larva]]e of the butterfly ''[[Marpesia petreus]]''.{{citation needed|date=March 2019}}

==Cultivation==
As the common name, "creeping fig" indicates, the plant has a creeping/vining habit and is often used in gardens and landscapes where it covers the ground and climbs up trees and walls. It is hardy down to {{convert| 1|C|F|abbr=on}}<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 39 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 27 February 2018}}</ref> and does not tolerate frost. Therefore, in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions it is often seen as a [[houseplant]]. It is fast-growing and requires little in the way of care. It can be invasive when environmental conditions are favorable. Its secondary roots or [[tendrils]] can cause structural damage to certain buildings with fragile [[Mortar (masonry)|mortar]] or structures made of fragile materials.

It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Ficus pumila'' AGM|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/7210/Ficus-pumila/Details |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=4 July 2020}}</ref>

==Varieties and cultivars==
*[[Ficus pumila var. awkeotsang|''Ficus pumila'' var. ''awkeotsang'']] —  awkeotsang creeping fig
*''Ficus pumila'' var. ''quercifolia'' —  oak leaf creeping fig
*''Ficus pumila'' 'Curly' — curly creeping fig; crinkled leaf form
*''Ficus pumila'' 'Variegata' and ''Ficus pumila'' 'Snowflake' — variegated creeping fig; [[variegated]]  foliage
*''Ficus pumila'' 'Minima' – features smaller, heart-shaped leaves<ref>[https://www.plantmark.com.au/ficus-pumila-minima Ficus pumila Minima] Plantmark. Accessed 14 December 2025.</ref>

== Cuisine ==
The fruit of [[Ficus pumila var. awkeotsang|''Ficus pumila'' var. ''awkeotsang'']] is used in cuisine. In [[Taiwan]], its fruit is turned inside out and dried. The seeds are scraped off and a gel is extracted from their surface with water and allowed to set and form a jelly known in Taiwan as ''[[aiyu jelly]]'' (or ''aiyuzi'' 愛玉子) and in [[Singapore]] as ''ice jelly'' (文頭雪).

==Toxicity==
Like other plant species in the family [[Moraceae]], contact with the milky sap of ''Ficus pumila'' can cause [[phytophotodermatitis]],<ref name="Rademaker and Derraik 2012">{{cite journal |last1=Rademaker |first1=M. |last2=Derraik |first2=J. G. |title=Phytophotodermatitis caused by ''Ficus pumila'' |journal=Contact Dermatitis |date=July 2012 |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=53–56 |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0536.2012.02026.x |pmid=22681467|s2cid=39421000 }}</ref> a potentially serious skin inflammation. Although the plant is not poisonous per se, ''F. pumila'' is listed in the FDA Database of Poisonous Plants.<ref>{{cite web |title=FDA Poisonous Plant Database |url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=8352 |publisher=U.S. Food & Drug Administration |access-date=11 December 2018 |archive-date=4 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221004024609/https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=8352 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
